edges.limitations: The mouse loses beta-cell mass postnatally through decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis - a developmental and survival failure. Human MANF-knockout beta-like cells develop normally and fail only under secretory challenge. Treating the mouse mechanism as the human one would predict a reduced beta-cell mass that the human data do not support, and would misdirect any therapeutic reasoning about beta-cell regeneration in these patients.

nodes.description:
Beta cells are under high demand for insulin synthesis, folding and secretion, and proinsulin folds in the ER before it can be packaged. That standing load is why the beta cell is where an ER stress buffer is worth most, and it is the reason a ubiquitously relevant chaperone deficit produces diabetes as its cardinal feature.
In MANF-knockout human beta-like cells the ER stress markers BiP, GRP170 and TXNIP trend upward and proinsulin accumulates. The stress is real but mild at baseline - the phenotype needs a challenge to become visible, which is the point of the next node.

nodes.description:
Severe short stature, bilateral sensorineural deafness, microcephaly and developmental delay accompany the diabetes and give the syndrome its name. The two patients have different homozygous variants and strikingly similar extrapancreatic features, which is itself an argument that these belong to the disease rather than to either family.
The authors do offer a reason, and it is an argument from company rather than a demonstration: the brain is sensitive to ER-stress-mediated damage and is almost always affected alongside the pancreas in the other ER-stress monogenic diabetes syndromes, so the same is inferred here. For the cochlea there is a mouse experiment - inner-ear MANF inactivation kills outer hair cells progressively with hearing loss - and Manf-null mice also show a growth defect independent of their diabetes. So the extrapancreatic arm has a proposed mechanism supported by analogy and by mouse data, and no measurement in these patients. The entry curates it at that strength; the residual uncertainty is a knowledge gap below.
One asymmetry between the two patients bears directly on the short stature: case 2 has partial hypopituitarism with growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone and gonadotropin deficiency, while case 1 had none by fourteen years of age. Short stature in this syndrome may therefore not have a single route even across two patients.

nodes.description:
The node that carries the actual human finding, and the one that distinguishes this disease from a developmental beta-cell disorder. MANF-null human beta-like cells develop normally; they fail when challenged.
The challenge experiments are discriminating rather than uniformly positive, which is informative about the mechanism. Tunicamycin (blocking N-linked glycosylation) and thapsigargin (depleting ER calcium) killed knockout and wild-type cells about equally. Brefeldin A, which blocks ER-to-Golgi cargo transfer, killed 29% of knockout cells against 18% of wild-type - a significant difference, and a modest one. So the vulnerability is not to ER stress in general but to a block in secretory export: a defect of the trafficking arm rather than of the folding arm.
Both numbers are stated deliberately. Against a wild-type baseline of 18%, this is a shift in susceptibility rather than a switch between survival and death, and an entry that reported only the 29% would imply a starker result than the experiment produced.
Transplantation supplies the in vivo counterpart: knockout grafts failed particularly in recipient mice that were themselves diabetic, i.e. under metabolic demand.

nodes.description: The rate-limiting state. MANF does not fold proteins; it attenuates the response to their misfolding. Losing it therefore does not create a folding defect, it removes a buffer - which is why the resulting disease is one of reduced tolerance rather than of baseline dysfunction, and why its severity should be expected to track folding demand across tissues.
